headline: Natsuku is from 馴れ付く (naretsuku, literally “to be attached intimately”).
Koji is from Middle Chinese 孤兒 (MC ku nye|ngej).
Masaru, “to excel”, is a doublet of 増さる (masaru, “to increase”).
Oyobi is the continuative stem of the verb 及ぶ (oyobu, “to reach”).
Hinomaru is 日 (hi, “sun”) plus の (no, attributive particle) plus 丸 (maru, “circle”).
Shitashirabe is 下 (shita-, “preliminary”) plus 調べ (shirabe), the stem of 調べる (shiraberu, “to investigate”).
Awasu is a doublet of 合わせる (awaseru), its conjugation shifted irregularly from the bigrade pattern.
Setsunai is 切 (setsu, “urgent, pressing, close”) plus ない (-nai, adjectivizing suffix).
Muko is found in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE with the spelling 聟, and may be from Proto-Japonic *moko.
Shareru may be a semantic shift from 曝れる (shareru), or derive from the classical verb 戯る (saru), and is first cited to a text from 1660.
Sakaeru is cognate with 盛る (sakaru, “to become frisky, to flourish”), ultimately deriving from 咲く (saku, “to bloom”).
Shozai is from Middle Chinese 所在 (MC srjoX dzojH).
ジャンパー is borrowed from English jumper.
Enman is from Chinese 圓滿 (yuánmǎn), a calque of a Sanskrit word.
Hareru is from Old Japanese, appears in the Man'yōshū of 759 CE, and is originally from the realis form of 張る (haru, “to become taut or tense”).
カンニング is a wasei eigo (pseudo-anglicism) derived from cunning.
Kaseki is 化 (ka, “to change into”) plus 石 (seki, “stone”).
Torii is 鳥 (tori, “bird”) plus 居 (i, “abode”), from old legends of birds sitting on tree branches, and is first cited to a text from 922 CE.
Akkenai is from 飽く気なし (aku ke nashi).
Jishu appeared in a pocket dictionary of English and Japanese from 1862.
Ayamachi is the continuative stem of the verb 過つ (ayamatsu, “to err, make a mistake”).
Kisen was probably coined in Japan from 汽 (ki, “steam”) plus 船 (sen, “boat, ship”).
Mochikiri is the continuative stem of the verb 持ち切る (mochikiru).
Tadōshi is 他動 (tadō, “other-moving, other-acting”) plus 詞 (shi, “word; part of speech”).
システム is from English system.
Hibana is 火 (hi, “fire”) plus 花 (hana, “flower”).
Shimiru is from Old Japanese 染む (“to dye”), an upper bigrade verb that became upper monograde.
ゼリー is from English jelly.
ジャズ is borrowed from English jazz.
Moriagaru is 盛る (moru) plus 上がる (agaru).
